School & learning

syntax noun

also construction (grammar), grammatical construction, constructions

late Latin

Prisc. 17.1.1 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 239, 248

syntaxis, syntaxis f.

noun, third declension

syntax, the connection of words

Priscian’s Greek word (σύνταξις). Traupman’s pupil answers how he knows a case: Ā syntaxī, from the syntax (239).

Other words

  • cōnstrūctiō, cōnstrūctiōnis f. — grammatical construction

    noun, third declension · also used · late Latin · Cic. Or. 37: verbōrum cōnstrūctiō (Lewis & Short); Prisc. p. 1061 P. (Lewis & Short); Traupman 246

    Cicero uses it of the arrangement of words in a sentence (verbōrum cōnstrūctiō et numerus, Or. 37, Lewis & Short); as the grammarian’s term for a construction it is Priscian’s. Cicero’s other phrase is cōnfōrmātiō verbōrum (de Or. 1.151, Lewis & Short).

  • 1ōrdinātiō: long o (Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked). From ōrdō, which the lexicon writes with a long o; Lewis & Short leaves both words unmarked.

    ōrdinātiō1, ōrdinātiōnis f. — syntax

    noun, third declension · also used · modern · Traupman 248

    Traupman offers it as the “pure Latin” word; Lewis & Short gives it of order and arrangement in general (Vitruvius, Pliny), not of words.

Examples

  • Unde hoc certum est? — Ā syntaxī.

    How is that certain? — From the syntax.Traupman 239

See also grammar, sentence, clause.

SourcesLewis & Short: syntaxis · Lewis & Short: constructio · Lewis & Short: ordinatio
